about.title: Santa Ana Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Santa Ana is the county seat of Orange County and home to roughly 335,400 people, many of whom earn a living in warehouses, on construction sites, in kitchens, and behind the wheel. A workplace injury here often starts simply: a fall from a ladder, a strained back on a loading dock, or a delivery run that ends in a collision on Bristol Street or 1st Street. The city recorded 1,708 injury collisions in 2025, with 2,383 people hurt, and some of those involved workers who were on the clock along I-5 or a surface street when the crash happened. Workers' compensation covers most on-the-job injuries no matter who was at fault, but it does not always account for everything you lost. When a subcontractor, a property owner, an equipment manufacturer, or another driver played a part, a separate third-party claim may be available. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect you with an independent attorney who can sort out which path fits your situation and explain what a contingency arrangement means for you.

whyChoose.title: Why Santa Ana Workers Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: We look past workers' comp
items.desc: In California, workers' comp is usually your only claim against your employer, regardless of fault. The attorneys we connect you with check whether a negligent third party, such as a subcontractor, property owner, or another driver, opens a separate claim.

items.title: Timing matters, and we move quickly
items.desc: California expects you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and any third-party claim carries a two-year deadline. A free connection today helps you stay ahead of both.

items.title: Your job is protected by law
items.desc: Retaliating against a worker for reporting an injury or filing a claim is illegal in California. An independent attorney can explain your rights if you are worried about pushback at work.

items.question: I was hit while driving for work on I-5 through Santa Ana. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were on the clock, workers' comp should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages no matter who caused the crash. If another driver was at fault, you may also have a separate third-party injury claim against that driver, which is subject to California's two-year deadline. An attorney can help you pursue the two side by side without one undermining the other.

items.question: What happens if I did not report my injury to my employer right away?
items.answer: California asks you to report a workplace injury within 30 days, so do it as soon as you can, ideally in writing. A late report does not always end your claim, but it can complicate it and invite disputes about how the injury happened. Talking to an attorney early helps you document things properly from here forward.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge me anything to get connected?
items.answer: No. Our service is free, and we are not a law firm. We connect you with an independent attorney who handles injury cases on contingency, which means there is no attorney fee unless there is a recovery. You decide whether to move forward after that first conversation.
